title: JavaScript closures: what they really remember
summary: You know what a closure is. Refresh what it actually remembers, and why loop callbacks and shared counters go wrong.
objective: Predict what a closure reads when it runs, and fix callbacks that share a variable they shouldn't.

options.feedback: That's what you'd get if each callback saved `i` when it was created. It doesn't.
The loop only stops once `i++` pushes `i` to 3, so 3 is its final value.
`i` still exists after the loop ends; the callbacks keep it alive.

hook.explanation: All three print 3. The callbacks run after the loop, and none of them remembers what `i` was when it was made. Why not?

bricks.title: Closures hold variables, not values
bricks.body: A closure is a function plus the variables in scope where it was written. It holds the **variables themselves**, not copies of their values. Reads and writes go straight to the variable, so a callback that runs later sees whatever the variable holds **then**, and two closures over one variable see each other's changes. In the hook, three callbacks share one `i`, and the loop has pushed it to 3 before any of them runs.

bricks.prompt: The button is clicked a minute after this code runs. What does `greet` receive?

options.feedback: The handler didn't save `user` when it was attached. It reads the variable at click time, when it points to the Linus object.
Reassigning `user` doesn't break the handler; the handler simply reads the new object.

bricks.explanation: The arrow reads `user` when the click happens. By then `user` points to the Linus object, so `greet` gets `'Linus'`.

options.feedback: `get` doesn't snapshot `balance` when it's created. It reads the same variable that `add` has been changing.
`add` adds to `balance` rather than replacing it, so both calls count.
`balance` lives on after `makeWallet` returns, because `add` and `get` still hold it.

bricks.explanation: `add` and `get` close over the same `balance`. Both calls to `add` change it, and `get` reads its current value: 15.

bricks.title: Each call makes fresh variables
bricks.body: Every call to a function creates **new** local variables, parameters included, and closures made during that call keep that set. Call it twice, get two independent sets. Blocks work the same way for `let` and `const`: a loop body, and a `for (let …)` header, make new ones on each pass. A `var` belongs to the whole function, so a `var` loop has one shared variable.

bricks.prompt: What does this log after 100 ms?

options.feedback: The arrow never mentions `count`. It reads `n`, a parameter that was set to 1 when `logLater` was called.
`n` still exists when the timer fires; the arrow keeps that call's variables alive.

bricks.hint: Which variable does the arrow function actually read?
bricks.explanation: The closure holds `n`, a fresh variable for that call, set to 1. Changing `count` afterwards doesn't touch `n`.

bricks.prompt: Complete the loop so each retry gets its own attempt number.

mistakes.feedback: A `var` is one variable for the whole function, so every retry reads its final value, 4.
`attempt++` can't reassign a `const`, so the loop throws a TypeError after the first pass.

bricks.explanation: `let` in a `for` header makes a new `attempt` on each pass, so each callback keeps its own: 1, 2, 3.

challenge.prompt: Every handler this returns shows the last tab. Which changes make each handler show its own tab?

options.text: Change `var i` to `let i`, and nothing else
options.feedback: The arrow reads `name`, not `i`. `name` is still a `var`, one for the whole function, holding the last tab.

options.text: Change `var i` to `let i`, and call `showTab(names[i])` inside the arrow
Keep `var i`, and call `showTab(names[i])` inside the arrow
options.feedback: Now the arrow reads `i`, a single shared `var`. When a handler runs, `i` equals `names.length`, so `names[i]` is `undefined`.

challenge.hint: For each change, ask which variable the arrow reads, and how many copies of it exist.
challenge.explanation: A fix works when the variable the arrow reads is fresh each pass: a block-scoped `name`, or a `let i` read directly. A shared `var` ends at the last value.

takeaways: A closure reads its variables when it runs, not when it was created.
Each function call, and each pass through a block with `let` or `const`, makes fresh variables; a `var` is one per function.
When a callback sees the wrong value, ask which variable it reads and how many copies of that variable exist.
